new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states where stress falls in Mintil as such. The collector of the only published Mintil data (Benjamin) describes Mintil words in terms of Aslian 'major syllables', which he glosses in the same paper as the stressed, word-final syllable; the family-wide generalisation (Dunn et al. 2011, quoted by Benjamin) is that the final syllable of the word always carries stress. Provisional reading: fixed word-final stress, inherited from the Northern Aslian / Menraq-Batek pattern (cf. first-hand final-stress statements for sister varieties Jedek, Jahai, Maniq, Kensiw), not from a Mintil-specific description.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Mintil. Benjamin notes Mintil-specific diphthongal/triphthongal nuclei in major (final) syllables and 'unique complex secondary changes in pronunciation' (1976: p. 51), Lye (2013, via Lim 2020) a distinctive 'intonation', but no one links these to stress placement.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (Aslian sesquisyllabic/iambic word; 'major syllable' = final syllable of the phonological word). Nothing on phrase-level prominence or citation forms. Dunn et al. 2011 explicitly had no Mintil data, so their statement reaches Mintil only by classification.
new_statements.identity_note: Mintil [mzt] = Batek Tanum/Tanɨm (Benjamin 2012, Lye 2013) = Mayah (Lim 2020) = Manya' (Tacey 2018); 'Mintil' is an exonym the speakers consider derogatory (Yager 2020: 30-31). Glottolog 5.1 lists it as a language sister to Batek (bate1262) within Batekic; Kruspe, Burenhult & Wnuk 2015 treat it as a dialect of Batek; Lim 2020 and Benjamin 1976 argue it is a distinct Menraq-Batek variety. Benjamin's data (the only published Mintil material) were collected from Gombak hospital patients in the late 1960s; Lim's 2017-2019 survey covers the Tanum valley settlements (e.g. Kampung Bencah Kelubi), Pahang. All stress statements found are family/genus-level (Aslian, Northern Aslian) or about sister varieties (Jedek, Jahai, Maniq, Kensiw), not Mintil itself.

sources.note: p. 167 + fn. 26: Benjamin's own late-1960s Mintil data; 'The major syllables of this language frequently consist of diphthongal and (uniquely in Aslian) sometimes triphthongal, nuclei'. p. 179 (sec. 4.2, Aslian-wide): 'major (i.e., stressed, word-final) vowel systems'. p. 187 (sec. 4.2.4) quotes Dunn et al. 2011: 300: the final syllable 'always receives stress'.
